title: Joshua 22:10–20
context: The eastern tribes build a large altar by the Jordan. Fearing rebellion against the LORD’s one altar, Israel gathers for war but first sends Phinehas and ten princes, who recall Peor and Achan as warnings of corporate judgment.

verses.text: When they came to the region near the Jordan, that is in the land of Canaan, the children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh built an altar there by the Jordan, a great altar to look at.
verses.arminianNotes: Near the Jordan the eastern tribes build a large altar. Arminian readers note that the narrative initially leaves their motive unstated, creating tension for the reader as well as for Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the altar’s size raising concern. The text delays explaining its purpose, so the reader experiences the same uncertainty as the western tribes.

verses.text: The children of Israel heard this, “Behold, the children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built an altar along the border of the land of Canaan, in the region around the Jordan, on the side that belongs to the children of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Israel hears, “Behold, the children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built an altar.” Arminian readers see a report that sparks alarm without full information.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see how quickly suspicion can arise. The verse records what Israel heard, not yet what the eastern tribes intended.

verses.text: When the children of Israel heard of it, the whole congregation of the children of Israel gathered themselves together at Shiloh, to go up against them to war.
verses.arminianNotes: The whole congregation gathers at Shiloh to go to war. Arminian readers see zeal for God’s worship, though the readiness for conflict shows the risk of acting before understanding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see serious concern for faithfulness to God’s single altar. The willingness to fight shows how seriously Israel took the danger of false worship.

verses.text: The children of Israel sent to the children of Reuben, and to the children of Gad, and to the half-tribe of Manasseh, into the land of Gilead, Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel sends Phinehas the son of Eleazar to Gilead. Arminian readers see a wise decision to investigate before attacking, sending a respected priest to speak first.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see prudence in seeking clarity. Phinehas was known for zeal at Peor in Numbers 25, which makes his role here as negotiator notable.

verses.text: With him were ten princes, one prince of a fathers’ house for each of the tribes of Israel; and they were each head of their fathers’ houses among the thousands of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Ten princes, one from each tribe, accompany Phinehas. Arminian readers see the whole nation represented, so the delegation speaks for all Israel rather than a faction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see representative leadership in action. The careful composition of the group shows the seriousness and fairness of the inquiry.

verses.text: They came to the children of Reuben, and to the children of Gad, and to the half-tribe of Manasseh, to the land of Gilead, and they spoke with them, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The delegation comes to Gilead and speaks with the eastern tribes. Arminian readers see dialogue chosen before force, giving the accused an opportunity to explain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see communication preceding judgment. The verse sets up the confrontation that follows in the delegation’s speech.

verses.text: “The whole congregation of the LORD says, ‘What trespass is this that you have committed against the God of Israel, to turn away today from following the LORD, in that you have built yourselves an altar, to rebel today against the LORD?
verses.arminianNotes: The delegation asks what “trespass” the eastern tribes have committed “against the God of Israel.” Arminian readers see sincere concern that the altar signals rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the accusation framed as turning away from the LORD. The question reflects a genuine fear for the covenant, though it assumes the worst before hearing a reply.

verses.text: Is the iniquity of Peor too little for us, from which we have not cleansed ourselves to this day, although there came a plague on the congregation of the LORD,
verses.arminianNotes: They recall the iniquity of Peor and the plague that followed. Arminian readers see past judgment remembered as a warning against repeating sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see corporate memory of Numbers 25 shaping present concern. The reference shows how one group’s sin affected the whole congregation.

verses.text: that you must turn away today from following the LORD? It will be, since you rebel today against the LORD, that tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: They warn that rebellion today will bring God’s anger on the whole congregation tomorrow. Arminian readers see concern for shared responsibility among God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the corporate dimension of covenant faithfulness. The warning expresses the conviction that sin within the community affects everyone.

verses.text: However, if the land of your possession is unclean, then pass over to the land of the possession of the LORD, in which the LORD’s tabernacle dwells, and take possession among us; but don’t rebel against the LORD, nor rebel against us, in building an altar other than the LORD our God’s altar.
verses.arminianNotes: They offer to share land west of the Jordan if the eastern land is unclean, but urge, “don’t rebel against the LORD.” Arminian readers see a generous offer aimed at restoring unity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a remarkable willingness to give up land for the sake of faithfulness. The offer shows the delegation’s concern for right worship rather than mere territorial control.

verses.text: Didn’t Achan the son of Zerah commit a trespass in the devoted thing, and wrath fell on all the congregation of Israel? That man didn’t perish alone in his iniquity.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: They ask whether Achan’s sin did not bring wrath on all Israel. Arminian readers see another historical example used to warn of corporate consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Joshua 7 recalled as a precedent. The phrase “That man didn’t perish alone in his iniquity” stresses how one person’s sin can affect the community.
